pages.text: Pinocchio

image.note: Cover: Geppetto and the wooden puppet coming to life

pages.text: Contents. The Puppet Who Came Alive / Pinocchio Runs Wild / The Fox and the Cat / The Land of Toys / Inside the Great Fish / A Real Boy.

Old Geppetto was a poor woodcarver who wished, more than anything, for a child of his own. So one evening he carved a little puppet boy out of a curious piece of wood, and named him Pinocchio. And that night, something quite impossible happened.

image.note: Geppetto carving the puppet by candlelight

pages.text: As Geppetto finished the last touches, the puppet's eyes blinked, its wooden mouth grinned, and it laughed out loud. Geppetto could hardly believe it. His puppet was alive! Pinocchio kicked his new legs, leapt from the bench, and ran straight out of the door into the street, quick as a flash.

image.note: Pinocchio leaping to life and running off

pages.text: Poor Geppetto chased him, caught him, and carried him home, more delighted than angry. "You shall be my son," he said, "and go to school, and grow good and wise." He sold his own coat to buy Pinocchio a school-book, for it was cold, and he loved the little puppet already.

image.note: Geppetto hugging Pinocchio, holding a book

pages.text: That night a small voice spoke from the corner. It was a Talking Cricket, old and wise. "Pinocchio," it said, "boys who will not listen, who run wild and tell lies, come to no good. Be good, work hard, and mind your father." But Pinocchio was in no mood to be told anything, and he did not listen at all.

image.note: The Talking Cricket advising Pinocchio

pages.text: The very next morning, on his way to school, Pinocchio heard drums and pipes. A puppet show! He forgot school at once, and to buy a ticket he sold the very school-book his father had given his coat for. "I'll go to school tomorrow," he told himself. "Just this once."

image.note: Pinocchio drawn away by the puppet show

pages.text: At the show the puppets welcomed him as one of their own, and the gruff showman, though fierce at first, heard about kind old Geppetto and let him go, even giving him five gold coins to carry home to his father. "Now I shall make Papa so happy," thought Pinocchio, setting off.

image.note: Pinocchio among the show-puppets

pages.text: But on the road he met a sly Fox and a sly Cat, who had seen his gold. "Five coins?" they purred. "Why, we know a magic field where, if you bury gold, it grows overnight into a tree of a thousand coins!" Pinocchio, who longed to be rich and clever, believed every word.

image.note: The sly Fox and Cat flattering Pinocchio

pages.text: Of course it was a trick, and the Fox and Cat took his gold and left him with nothing. When at last he found a kind blue-haired Fairy and she asked what had become of his coins, Pinocchio, ashamed, began to lie. "They were stolen," he said, "far away, by robbers."

image.note: Pinocchio fibbing to the blue Fairy

pages.text: And as he lied, the strangest thing happened. His nose began to grow. With each new fib it grew longer and longer, right across the room, until it was so long he could not turn his head. The Fairy watched, and smiled sadly. "You see, Pinocchio," she said, "lies are soon found out. They always show."

image.note: Pinocchio's nose growing with each lie

pages.text: Pinocchio wept and promised to be good, and the Fairy forgave him and made his nose right again. "Go home to your father," she said, "and go to school, and be honest, and one day you may become a real boy." A real boy! It was Pinocchio's dearest wish, and he ran off, meaning truly to be good this time.

image.note: The Fairy comforting a sorry Pinocchio

pages.text: But being good is hard when you never listen, and Pinocchio was easily led. A boy told him of a wonderful place called the Land of Toys, where there was no school, no work, only play from morning to night, all day, every day, for ever. It sounded like heaven, and off Pinocchio went.

image.note: Pinocchio boarding a coach to the Land of Toys

pages.text: For a while it was glorious: games and sweets and no lessons at all. But there was a dreadful secret in that land. Boys who did nothing but play, and never worked or learned a thing, slowly, over the idle weeks, began to change. It started, of all things, with their ears.

image.note: Boys playing wildly in the Land of Toys

pages.text: One morning Pinocchio woke to a terrible itch, put up his hand, and felt, growing from his own head, two long furry donkey's ears. He had idled like all the rest, and now he was changing too. Frightened at last, he understood the cricket had been right all along, and he fled that dreadful place as fast as he could.

image.note: Pinocchio horrified, feeling long ears

pages.text: Racing home, truly sorry now, Pinocchio learned that Geppetto had sailed out to sea to search for him, and had been swallowed whole by an enormous fish, as big as a ship. Without a moment's pause, brave now where once he was selfish, Pinocchio dived into the waves to find his father.

image.note: Pinocchio diving into stormy waves

pages.text: The same great fish swallowed Pinocchio too, and there, in the dark cavern of its belly, by the light of a little candle, sat old Geppetto, thin and frightened, but alive. "My boy!" he cried. "My Pinocchio!" and the two hugged as though they would never let go.

image.note: Pinocchio finding Geppetto inside the fish

pages.text: "Now we must escape," said Pinocchio, and this time it was the puppet who was brave and clever. He waited until the great fish slept with its huge mouth open, took his weak father on his back, and swam, out through the great jaws and up, up to the surface and the open air.

image.note: Pinocchio carrying Geppetto out of the fish's mouth

pages.text: Pinocchio swam his father safely to shore, and from that day he was changed. He worked hard to care for old Geppetto, went to school at last, told the truth, and thought of his father before himself. The wild, selfish puppet had become kind, honest, and brave.

image.note: Pinocchio working hard to care for Geppetto

pages.text: One morning he woke, and something felt different. He put his hand to his face, and it was not wood, but warm skin. He ran to the mirror and could not believe his eyes. Looking back at him was not a puppet at all, but a real, living boy, with bright eyes and rosy cheeks.

image.note: Pinocchio the real boy at the mirror

pages.text: The blue Fairy's promise had come true. Because he had learned to be good, and honest, and to love another before himself, Pinocchio was a real boy at last. And in the corner sat the old wooden puppet he had once been, propped up and still smiling, as if glad to have carried him so far.

image.note: Real boy Pinocchio, wooden puppet resting nearby

pages.text: Old Geppetto wept for joy, and hugged his son, his real son now, at last. The woodcarver who wished for a child had one, and the puppet who wished to be a boy had become one, and both had learned that the wish comes true not by magic, but by love, and courage, and doing what is right.

image.note: Geppetto embracing his real boy

pages.text: Pinocchio's lessons. Listen to those who love you. Do not run from school and work. A lie always shows, in the end. And a real boy, or girl, is made not of magic, but of honesty, kindness, and courage. Old Geppetto knew it, the Talking Cricket knew it, and, at last, so did Pinocchio.

image.note: Pinocchio, Geppetto, and the cricket together
